subject: Convergence issues in complex hierachical model

messages.author: b17f4d0880547804
messages.subject: Convergence issues in complex hierachical model
parts:
Hi,
I'm having problems with some of the parameters converging in one of my hierarchical models. I think it may have something to do with hyper parameter correlations... particularly among the sigmas... and I was wondering if anyone has any suggestions on how to improve the sampling.

What the model attempts to do is estimate plant mortality as a function of growth dependent and growth independent processes.
The growth dependent part of the model is essentially a negative exponential, where the probability of dying decreases log_alpha (which describes the probability of dying when growth is zero). The rate of decline in mortality hazard is defined by log_beta.
Because the probability of death is never truly zero I also have an asymptote parameter (log_gamma).
We expect these parameters to be independent of each other. 

What I wanted to do is have each of these parameters vary by species (i.e. log_a0, log_b0, log_c0), census (time) period (i.e. log_a1, log_b1, log_c1), and another covariate (log_a2, log_b2, log_c2).

growth_measure is data and is scaled by 1 SD. I'm planning on running the model for several kinds of growth measures. On the standardised scale these growth measures very from 0-10 or 0-60 with the bulk of the data occurring at the lower end of these ranges.  

What I'm finding is that the model struggles to sample some parameters after 2000 iterations (see attached trace plot).
I've implemented a non-centered parameterisation I've also put the model parameters on the log scale to reduce arithmetic overflow/underflow issues. I've increased the adapt delta to 0.9 and lowered the stepsize to 0.1. I've also increased the tree depth to 15 - to ensure I'm not hitting the upper limit.

At the moment the model settles on a stepsize of 7.942807e-03 and takes 511 leapfrogs (9 treedepth).

I've also used fairly informative priors defined either by previous literature (e.g. priors on log_mu_a0, log_sigma_a0, log_mu_c0 and log_sigma_c0) or from what I think is a biological reasonable parameter space (all other parameters, particularly those on log_beta). The normal(0,2.5) priors I fitted for log_mu_b0 and log_b2 were chosen so that the relationship between growth and mortality can be very steep or very shallow.

From looking at the pairs plots (also attached) and traceplots... I think the issue is to do with correlations between the species level sigmas. But I'm not sure.
I guess it could also be due to the priors on the sigma's being too large (I struggle to think in log space)... but this is difficult to test as the model takes a reasonably long time to complete and the convergence problem isn't apparent when I run the model on smaller subsets of data.

I'm attempting to fit this model to a large amount of data (100,000 + observations). The species random effect (e.g. log_a0) consists of 203 groups, whereas the time random effect (e.g. log_a1) consists of three groups.

I've attempted to vectorise as much as possible. Also, incase someone asks... I've used the increment_log_prob because I don't think stan currently has bernoulli_cloglog(). The clog log is useful for survival analyses such as this and has a few advantages in terms of interpretation over the logit.

I'm seriously at a loss as to what to do next besides running the model for more iterations - which I'm hesitant to do as it will greatly increase wall time... and I'm not sure it will solve the underlying problem (as the chains don't appear to be converging in some cases).


Also thanks to Bob who has helped me get this far!
Cheers
J

On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 12:50:49 AM UTC-4, James Camac wrote:

Excellent use of pairs(). In this case, there is only 1 divergent transition when accept_stat__ is above is median but several (indicated by red points) when accept_stat__ is below its median. To me, this often suggests a (possibly numeric) problem with the model in the tails. (If the situation were reversed, I would just say keep making adapt_delta higher until the problem goes away). It seems that log_sigma_b0 has a bimodal posterior, which is not ideal for sampling, and some of the other log_sigma terms are bunched up against the lower bound of zero (For plotting purposes, it may be better to generate the logarithm of log_sigma_* in the generated quantities block and put these unbounded parameters into your pairs plot rather than their constrained counterparts). If it is not plausible to you that the log_sigma_* terms could be zero, then a different prior could help. Andrew is a great champion of these half-Cauchy priors but they do have a mode at zero.

I've attempted to vectorise as much as possible. Also, incase someone asks... I've used the increment_log_prob because I don't think stan currently has bernoulli_cloglog(). The clog log is useful for survival analyses such as this and has a few advantages in terms of interpretation over the logit.

Stan currently does not have a bernoulli_cloglog(). I would try to encapsulate all that code that results in the log-likelihood into a user-defined Stan function, use expose_stan_functions() to export it to R, and verify that it agrees with

sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = binomial(link = 'cloglog')$linkinv(eta), log = TRUE))

Ben

parts:
On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 1:41:46 AM UTC-4, James Camac wrote:
I don’t think any of the sigma terms could be truly zero. So maybe a different set of priors would be more suitable.

For scale parameters, I do
  • Jeffreys if I know the units of measurement don't matter
  • rescaled Exponential if I know the mean
  • rescaled Gamma, Generalized Gamma, or Amoroso if I know more than the mean (which is rare)

Bounded or unbounded uniforms do not work well in cases like yours where the posterior density is concentrated near a bound because the transformation to the unconstrained space puts the unconstrained parameter too close to - or + infinity.


Ben

if (y[i] == 0) {

increment_log_prob(log_cumulative_hazard);
      } else {
        increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(log_cumulative_hazard));
      }

I’ve never understood these log log link functions that show up in
survival models but they make me queasy every time I see them —
they’re just asking for numerical problems.

Also, the really tight priors you have on the hierarchical means
could cause problems if they are inconsistent with the data (the
resulting posterior will be really, really narrow and require the
super small step size).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Convergence issues in complex hierachical model
parts:
Hi Michael,
What I'm trying to do is have build a model with additive hazards (the negative exponential defined by alpha and beta) and the independent term gamma.

Originally I had the following form:
log(-log(1-p)) = log(census_length) + log(alpha * exp(-beta * growth measure) + gamma)
where 
p = 1- exp(-(census_length * alpha * exp(-beta * growth measure) + gamma

But due to numerical instabilities and avoiding hard constraints I put this on the log scale.
In stan I implemented this like this

p[i] <- inv_cloglog(log(census_length[i] * (exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(b_log[i]) * growth_dt_s[i]) + exp(c_log[i]))));

However, this model was still full of numerical instabilities. The solution was to do some algebra to reduce the logging and exponentiating associated with the inv_cloglog function. (Hopefully I haven't stuffed the maths up).

Pr(y=1) = 1 - exp(-lambda x T)
where
lambda =exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(log_beta[i]) * growth_measure[i]) + exp(log_gamma[i]))
and T = census_length[i]

Pr(y=0) = 1 - Pr(y=1) = 1 - (1- exp(-lambda x T) = exp(-lambda x T)

We then add a log to each (conforming with our original model form).
Pr(y=1) = log(1-exp(-lambda x T) 

Pr(y=0) = log(exp(-lambda x T) = -lambda x T

I then use the increment_log_prob() and the log1m_exp() to calculate the likelihood.

cumulative_hazard[i] <- -census_length[i] * (exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(log_beta[i]) * growth_measure[i]) + exp(log_gamma[i]));

      if (y[i] == 0) {
        increment_log_prob(cumulative_hazard[i]);
      } else {
        increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard[i]));
      }
    }
Hopefully I've explained this ok... (these models make me queasy too!)

In terms of the priors around the log_mu_a0 and log_mu_c0 these are informed by other datasets and on the survival scale they aren't really that tight. 
For example
log_a0_mu ~ normal(-0.87,0.75)
means that 95% of the posterior encompasses the probability of dying from

1-exp(-exp(-0.87 + 1.5)) = p =0.84 chance of dying
whereas
1-exp(-exp(-0.87 - 1.5)) = p =0.09 chance of dying

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Convergence issues in complex hierachical model
parts:
Your likelihood has _three_ nested exponentials which drastically
amplify any perturbation of the underlying parameters (I thought these
models usually only had two — ugh).  The gradients are going to be huge 
and require really small step sizes, as you see.  And then you add a huge 
number of parameters and make everything worse — even if the marginal 
posterior for each parameters is reasonably well-behaved the probability 
that at least one of them varies to an extreme in a sample grows with the 
number of parameters.  It’s going to be really hard to avoid divergences and 
explore everything.

I’m not sure what to tell you.  Maybe others have suggestions for 
reparameterizations.
On Jul 21, 2015, at 11:15 AM, James Camac <james...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Michael,
What I'm trying to do is have build a model with additive hazards (the negative exponential defined by alpha and beta) and the independent term gamma.

Originally I had the following form:
log(-log(1-p)) = log(census_length) + log(alpha * exp(-beta * growth measure) + gamma)
where 
p = 1- exp(-(census_length * alpha * exp(-beta * growth measure) + gamma

But due to numerical instabilities and avoiding hard constraints I put this on the log scale.
In stan I implemented this like this

p[i] <- inv_cloglog(log(census_length[i] * (exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(b_log[i]) * growth_dt_s[i]) + exp(c_log[i]))));

However, this model was still full of numerical instabilities. The solution was to do some algebra to reduce the logging and exponentiating associated with the inv_cloglog function. (Hopefully I haven't stuffed the maths up).

Pr(y=1) = 1 - exp(-lambda x T)
where
lambda =exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(log_beta[i]) * growth_measure[i]) + exp(log_gamma[i]))
and T = census_length[i]

Pr(y=0) = 1 - Pr(y=1) = 1 - (1- exp(-lambda x T) = exp(-lambda x T)

We then add a log to each (conforming with our original model form).
Pr(y=1) = log(1-exp(-lambda x T) 

Pr(y=0) = log(exp(-lambda x T) = -lambda x T

I then use the increment_log_prob() and the log1m_exp() to calculate the likelihood.

cumulative_hazard[i] <- -census_length[i] * (exp(log_alpha[i] - exp(log_beta[i]) * growth_dt[i]) + exp(log_gamma[i]));

      if (y[i] == 0) {
        increment_log_prob(cumulative_hazard[i]);
      } else {
        increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard[i]));
      }
    }

Hopefully I've explained this ok... (these models make me queasy too!)

In terms of the priors around the log_mu_a0 and log_mu_c0 these are informed by other datasets and on the survival scale they aren't really that tight. 
For example
log_a0_mu ~ normal(-0.87,0.75)
means that 95% of the posterior encompasses the probability of dying from

1-exp(-exp(-0.87 + 1.5)) = p =0.84 chance of dying
whereas
1-exp(-exp(-0.87 - 1.5)) = p =0.09 chance of dying

On Tuesday, July 21, 2015 at 6:15:27 AM UTC-4, James Camac wrote:
However, this model was still full of numerical instabilities. The solution was to do some algebra to reduce the logging and exponentiating associated with the inv_cloglog function. (Hopefully I haven't stuffed the maths up).
Don't hope, verify. Make the log-likelihood into a user-defined Stan function, use expose_stan_functions() to export it to R, and verify that it agrees with
sum(dbinom(y, size = 1, prob = binomial(link = 'cloglog')$linkinv(eta), log = TRUE))

There is no Jeffreys prior in the Stan manual because it is often not a proper distribution. And it really only makes sense for a scalar scale parameter, in which case you can do

increment_log_prob(-log(scale_parameter));

Ben

messages.author: b17f4d0880547804
messages.subject: Dealing with correlated parameters in a hierarchical framework
parts:
Hi all,
I've finally managed to get back to this model and have ironed out a few issues.

I've made several changes to the model... but the root cause of the problem was as Ben pointed out the issue was to do with the variance parameters associated with a1,b1 and c1 bounding up against zero.
Removing those parameters and the model fits fine with no divergence. Also the model converges fairly quickly and for most parameters I have effect samples in the 100's for almost all parameters (the exception is log_b1_sigma where I have approx 80 after 1000 iterations (not too bad).

The issue I have now is whether there is something I can do to minimise the correlation between mu_log_a0 and mu_log_b0 and a2 and b2 (see pairs plot)...
While the model converges fine... interpreting what these parameters are doing is complicated by this correlation.

I'm guessing I could use some multivariate distribution between a0 and b0 and again between a2 and b2... but I have no idea how and where it should be implemented.
Any suggestions?

data {
        int<lower=1> n_obs;
        int<lower=1> n_spp;
        int<lower=1> spp[n_obs];
        int<lower=1> n_census;
        int<lower=1> census[n_obs];
        int<lower=0, upper=1> y[n_obs];
        vector[n_obs] census_length;
        vector[n_obs] growth_dt;
vector[n_spp] rho_c;

}
      
      parameters { 
        
      // Mortality model parameters

real raw_log_a0[n_spp];
      real mu_log_a0;
      real<lower=0> sigma_log_a0;

      real raw_log_b0[n_spp];
      real mu_log_b0;
      real<lower=0> sigma_log_b0;

      real raw_log_c0[n_spp];
      real mu_log_c0;
      real<lower=0> sigma_log_c0;

      real a2;
      real b2;
      real c2;

}
  
      model {
        
    // Declaring mortality parameters

real alpha;
    real a0[n_spp];

    real beta;
    real b0[n_spp];

    real gamma;
    real c0[n_spp];

real cumulative_hazard;

    // Calculating species random effects
    for (s in 1:n_spp) {

a0[s] <- exp(raw_log_a0[s] * sigma_log_a0 + mu_log_a0); // e.g. implies lognormal(mu_log_a0, sigma_log_a0)
      b0[s] <- exp(raw_log_b0[s] * sigma_log_b0 + mu_log_b0);
      c0[s] <- exp(raw_log_c0[s] * sigma_log_c0 + mu_log_c0);

}

    for (i in 1:n_obs) {
      // Calculating mortality parameters

alpha <- a0[spp[i]] * pow(rho_c[spp[i]], a2); 
      beta <- b0[spp[i]] * pow(rho_c[spp[i]], b2); 
      gamma <- c0[spp[i]] * pow(rho_c[spp[i]], c2);
// Likelihood for hazard model
cumulative_hazard <- -census_length[i] * (alpha * exp(-beta * growth_dt[i]) + gamma);
if (y[i] == 0) {

increment_log_prob(cumulative_hazard);
      } else {
        increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(cumulative_hazard));
      }
    }

    // Priors

    //Mortality model priors

raw_log_a0 ~ normal(0,1);
    mu_log_a0 ~ normal(-0.61, 0.57);
    sigma_log_a0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

    raw_log_b0 ~ normal(0, 1);
    mu_log_b0 ~ normal(0, 5);
    sigma_log_b0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

    raw_log_c0 ~ normal(0, 1);
    mu_log_c0 ~ normal(-3.86, 0.2);
    sigma_log_c0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

    a2 ~ normal(0,5);
    b2 ~ normal(0,5);
    c2 ~ normal(0,5);
      }

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dealing with correlated parameters in a hierarchical framework
parts:
I was hoping someone better at this kind of modeling than me would
answer, but here goes my try.

You could take these

> mu_log_a0 ~ normal(-0.61, 0.57);
> sigma_log_a0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>
> raw_log_b0 ~ normal(0, 1);
> mu_log_b0 ~ normal(0, 5);
> sigma_log_b0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
>
> raw_log_c0 ~ normal(0, 1);
> mu_log_c0 ~ normal(-3.86, 0.2);
> sigma_log_c0 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

and give them hierarchical multivariate (or even hierarchical univariate)
priors across a, b, and c. The problem is that you only have three draws, so
I doubt it's going to get you much, if anything, other than a computational headache.

I don't know if it make sense to have the raw versions, which are vectors,
get hierarchical priors --- are they normal(0, 1) to identify a scale and
location?

- Bob
